A Shia dynasty from Daylam, the mountains south of the Caspian Sea, that ruled most of Iran and Iraq from 934 to 1062. Three brothers, soldiers of fortune, built it; in 945 one of them took Baghdad and kept the Abbasid caliph as a figurehead.

The Buyids belong to what historians call the Iranian Intermezzo, when Iranian dynasties ruled between the Arab and Turkish eras. Their greatest ruler, Adud al-Dawla, united the family lands and built a hospital in Baghdad and a great dam near Shiraz. They were patrons of science and Persian culture, and Shia festivals were first held in public under them.

The family split into rival branches. In 1055 the Seljuk Tughril entered Baghdad, and the Seljuks took the last Buyid lands soon after. The map's Buyid Emirate shows them at their height around 1000. In the 1200 snapshot this label sits on a patch in the Pamir and Hindu Kush, far from Buyid lands and long after the dynasty ended, so it is best read as a mapping slip.
